title: nrpe-custom
text: Build and test custom NRPE packages for Debian and SUSE Linux Enterprise Server (SLES). Use a keyboard-driven menu or scriptable CLI to rebuild distribution packages with command argument support, then verify the result in an isolated container. Argument support is compiled in, but remains disabled at runtime by default. Enabling it on a server is an explicit administrator decision. Bash command substitution stays disabled. This is an independent project. Its packages are unofficial custom builds, not releases supported or certified by Debian, SUSE, or Nagios. Successful master pushes publish verified package releases ; remaining work and release evidence are tracked in the release plan . Independently authored project code and documentation are MIT licensed ; generated packages retain their upstream and distribution licenses . Use them at your own risk. The source code and build recipes are available for inspection and independent compilation. No malicious functionality is intended or knowingly included; this is not a guarantee that the project, its dependencies, or generated packages are free of defects or vulnerabilities. Review and test the software in your environment, retain backups, and plan recovery before production deployment. See deployment security and limitations . Quick start Install Git, Python 3.9+ , and Docker Engine with Linux containers, BuildKit, and Docker Compose 2.17+ . On Windows, start Docker Desktop and wait for its Linux engine to become ready. Make sure python3 --version works in your shell. ARM hosts need linux/amd64 emulation. Allow disk space for separate builder and test images; Docker's vfs storage driver can consume considerably more space. git clone https://github.com/NoJokeFNA/nrpe-custom.git cd nrpe-custom python3 nrpe.py doctor python3 nrpe.py verify debian12 This builds the package and tests its installation and NRPE argument handling. Find packages in output/<target>/ and run reports in .nrpe/runs/<run-id>/ . Builds and tests install packages inside containers, not on your workstation. Prefer nrpe.py : it coordinates this project's Compose files, checks Docker, protects targets against concurrent runs, and records logs and test results. Interactive menu Install the optional menu dependencies in your Python environment: python3 -m pip install -r requirements-menu.txt python3 nrpe.py Use ↑/↓ and Enter to navigate, Space to toggle targets, A to select all, and Esc to go back. Select build/test actions, diagnose Docker, inspect status, or choose a previous run's logs. Select an optional company CA certificate through its browser, or enter/paste its path directly. The menu reviews your choices before running and returns after each command. It retains choices within the session, shows real workflow phases and results, and offers log diagnosis and preview-first cleanup. Use / to filter lists; Windows drives live in a separate Switch drive... selector so many attached drives do not crowd out files. Colors highlight selection and errors; NO_COLOR enables monochrome output. See menu installation and controls , including virtual environments. Direct commands do not require the menu dependencies. Without an interactive terminal, launching without arguments prints help and never prompts. The affected deployment is SLES 12 SP3 , with old NRPE 2.15/OpenSSL 1.0.2. The previous SLES-15 target was based on an incorrect platform assumption and has been replaced. See the SLES guide and FAQ for the native rebuild and TLS/service diagnosis. Supported targets All package outputs target linux/amd64 ( x86_64 for RPM). Target Distribution Package Source policy debian11 Debian 11 Bullseye nagios-nrpe-server .deb Discover through APT; archived security packages debian12 Debian 12 Bookworm nagios-nrpe-server .deb Discover through APT debian13 Debian 13 Trixie nagios-nrpe-server .deb Discover through APT debian14 Debian 14 Forky nagios-nrpe-server .deb Discover through APT; moving testing suite sles12sp3 SLES 12 SP3 nrpe .rpm + companion user RPM Reviewed, pinned OBS sources; genuine SLES base Target availability depends on distribution repositories and image availability. A listed target is not a promise of ongoing upstream security maintenance. In particular, historical archives do not extend a distribution's support period. The SLES target uses a pinned genuine 12.3 image and verified original SLE-12 inputs; no ISO, SLE-15 packages or replacement distribution is used. Its native build and certificate-authenticated TLS 1.2 integration passed locally on 2026-10-28. Container results do not establish production deployment readiness. Use your run reports to identify the exact tested package bytes. Commands Command Action python3 nrpe.py doctor Check project files, Docker, Linux containers, and Compose python3 nrpe.py verify debian12 Build, validate, install, and integration-test python3 nrpe.py build debian12 Build and validate the exported package python3 nrpe.py test debian12 Install and test an existing local package python3 nrpe.py status Show artifacts, matching test results, and locks; no Docker needed python3 nrpe.py logs --last Show the most recent run's log python3 nrpe.py logs --run <id> Show a specific run's log Commands accept multiple targets or all by itself. all includes SLES. Use --help or <command> --help for details. Existing packages require confirmation before rebuilding. For automation, use --rebuild explicitly. --pull checks for updated base images; it does not check whether a built NRPE package is current. Debian source versions are discovered when building; SLES sources stay pinned until reviewed and updated. python3 nrpe.py verify debian12 debian13 --pull python3 nrpe.py verify sles12sp3 --rebuild python3 nrpe.py test debian11 For company HTTPS inspection, optionally select a local public CA certificate (PEM or DER); TLS verification remains enabled: python3 nrpe.py verify sles12sp3 -- ca - cert "C:\Certificates\Company-Root.cer" No certificate is required by default or included in the exported NRPE package. See company CA setup and Docker trust limits . The compatibility entry point build.py still works. See the workflow reference for flags, outputs, caching, logs, checksums, locks, and interruption handling. How it works How it works · Open full size View diagram source flowchart TD U[Menu or direct CLI] --> C[Controller: Docker checks and target lock] C --> A{Action} A -->|build or verify| B[Builder: fetch, build, validate, and export] B --> P[Controller: verify artifact identity and checksums] A -->|test existing package| P P --> T{Integration requested?} T -->|test or verify| I[Fresh matching runtime container] I --> D[TLS request: arguments rejected with runtime setting 0] D --> E[TLS requests: exact argument responses with runtime setting 1] E --> R[Artifact-bound report and logs] T -->|build only| R Each target has a builder image and a separate runtime test image. This prevents compilers and build dependencies from masking missing runtime dependencies. Docker reuses cached layers; images do not need to be recreated on every run. The client is check_nrpe , as used by Nagios; a complete Nagios server is not needed to test this protocol. Tests use TLS over loopback, publish no NRPE port, and leave the packaged default configuration unchanged. Installation success alone does not prove argument handling works. The test must reject arguments with dont_blame_nrpe=0 , then return exact results for two different argument pairs with dont_blame_nrpe=1 . Tests do not cover a full systemd boot, production certificates, or external Nagios connectivity. See architecture and file responsibilities for the component map and network requirements for firewall planning. Using a built package For NRPE installation concepts and server/client setup, consult the official NRPE documentation and the Nagios Core documentation . This project documents installing its custom distribution packages; it does not provide a complete Nagios/NRPE deployment guide. Monitoring-server setup, check_nrpe , plugin installation, check definitions, production TLS, and network access must be configured for your environment using the upstream and distribution documentation. Upstream source-install instructions describe an alternative installation method; do not install over the custom package with make install . Follow the installation guide for step-by-step Debian 11–14 and SLES 12 SP3 instructions: which files to copy, checksum verification, APT/zypper installation, the SLES companion user package, service startup, and installed-version checks. Run installation commands on the destination server. The guide also explains the unsigned custom RPMs and matching repository requirements. See SLES background for source provenance and historical repository availability. Before changing an existing server, read updates and rollback . Use the configuration examples for fixed checks, TLS settings and an optional restricted argument-profile wrapper. The support and maintenance policy explains tested boundaries, dependency monitoring and target deprecation. Review the server's configuration before enabling arguments: Distribution Configuration Service Debian /etc/nagios/nrpe.cfg nagios-nrpe-server SLES/OBS recipe /etc/nrpe.cfg nrpe allowed_hosts = <nagios-server-ip>,127.0.0.1,::1 dont_blame_nrpe = 1 Replace the placeholder, define permitted commands with validated arguments, configure trusted TLS certificates, and restrict the firewall to the intended monitoring servers before restarting the service. Keep Bash command substitution disabled. See deployment security . Development and project documentation master is the default/release branch; develop is the integration branch. Work on feat/... , fix/... , refactor/... or remove/... and open a PR into develop . Never delete master or develop . See the Git workflow . Successful master pushes build/test all five package targets and publish a complete release bundle ; other branches do not publish. GitHub Actions provides Linux/Windows unit and configuration checks and a scheduled Python dependency audit . These checks do not replace package builds and runtime integration tests. Menu guide : installation, keys, accessibility, and terminal behavior. Workflow reference : commands, artifacts, reports, and troubleshooting. Installation guide : deploy custom Debian/SLES packages and configure services. Updates and rollback : retain packages/configuration and recover deployments. Configuration examples : fixed checks, TLS and restricted argument profiles. Support and maintenance : verification boundaries, dependencies and source updates. Container layout : separate build/test recipes under docker/ . Git workflow : human authorship, integration, promotion and guarded branch cleanup. Release automation : per-master-push packages, sources, licenses and verification. Architecture : control flow and every script's purpose. Network requirements : domains, ports, directions, and proxy notes. FAQ : Nagios/NRPE service startup and when a custom build is needed. SLES 12 SP3 : provenance, dependencies, build inputs, TLS 1.2 and installation. SLES 12 SP3 handshake diagnostic : anonymized temporary NRPE 2.15 plaintext test and cleanup, without changing the production service. Contributing : development and meaningful validation. Security : argument risks and safe issue reporting. Release and maintenance plan : open work and future release requirements. Release history : published versions and exact validation evidence. Local cleanup : preview expired runs and explicitly selected retired outputs/images. Troubleshooting : contextual build hints and read-only diagnosis of NRPE/server logs. Documentation website : local preview, field notes and reviewed publication to GitHub Pages. These recipes provide a repeatable workflow, not a claim of bit-for-bit reproducibility. Sources, image tags, and repositories can change. Review upstream security updates and retain provenance with the artifacts you deploy.

title: Contributing
text: Read AGENTS.md and the more specific instructions under scripts/ and tests/ . Use the existing checkout and preserve unrelated local changes. Write code, comments, documentation, and commits in English. Development is independent of editors and operating systems; examples use python3 . Development checks Direct CLI commands need Python 3.9+ and no third-party Python packages. Install requirements-menu.txt to work on terminal navigation and run its keyboard tests. Builds and installation tests require Docker Engine, Linux containers, BuildKit, and Compose 2.17+. From the repository root: python3 -m pip install -r requirements-menu.txt python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v python3 nrpe.py doctor For shell syntax checks in Bash, check each script explicitly: for script in scripts/*.sh examples/*.sh ; do bash -n " $script " || exit ; done Without menu dependencies, terminal-input tests are reported as skipped. Workflow unit tests must remain independent of Docker and network access. Shell syntax and unit tests alone do not establish that packages build or arguments work. For a changed build or installation path, run the appropriate targets: python3 nrpe.py verify debian12 python3 nrpe.py verify sles12sp3 Use --rebuild only when replacing existing artifacts intentionally. Validate all affected targets when changing shared packaging behavior. Report exactly which checks ran, passed, failed, or were skipped, with any platform limitations. Native Windows terminal and process behavior need Windows verification; tests on Linux do not establish that Windows has been exercised. Design boundaries GitHub Actions runs the unit suite on Linux/Windows with Python 3.9 and 3.14, plus Linux shell syntax and both Compose configuration checks. The separate weekly dependency audit checks the optional menu requirements. Neither workflow performs package/protocol integration tests. See the maintenance policy and inspect actual workflow results for the commit under review. Container recipes live under docker/ ; their build context remains the repository root and Compose files remain at that root. Update Compose, doctor , and documentation together when moving a recipe. Keep UI navigation in nrpe_cli/menu.py ; use the existing controller for work. Preserve runtime-disabled argument defaults and disabled Bash substitution. Keep TLS, repository signatures, source checksums, and RPM verification enabled. Match the real target distribution; do not substitute Leap packages for SLES. Preserve separate builder/runtime images and meaningful protocol tests. Never install the build outputs on the development host during tests. Keep artifacts, ISO files, credentials, caches, and local reports out of Git. Before removing or combining scripts, consult the script responsibility review . Fewer files is not a goal if it couples independent package formats or removes useful verification boundaries. Changes and pull requests Start from develop on feat/... , fix/... , refactor/... , or remove/... . Open a PR into develop ; promote develop to master by PR. Never delete either long-lived branch or work directly on it. Use only the human commit author, with no co-author or generated-with/by attribution. See the Git workflow for route/author checks, guarded topic deletion and required administrator setup. Keep changes focused and commit independently reviewable changes separately. Use Conventional Commits , for example feat(menu): add target navigation or docs: clarify firewall rules . Describe the problem, resulting behavior, and actual validation in pull requests. Include relevant logs with private paths, addresses, and credentials removed. Use GitHub issues for reproducible non-sensitive bugs and feature proposals. For security-sensitive reports, follow the security guidance . Independently authored project code and documentation use the MIT license . Retain all third-party notices; see the license inventory . Public binary release preparation follows the release plan . It does not authorize publication or grant new rights to third-party code.

title: Third-party provenance and license inventory
text: This inventory records evidence inspected during release and website preparation on 2026-10-27 through 2026-10-29. It is not a completed redistribution approval. The root MIT license applies to independently authored project code and documentation; it does not relicense NRPE, distribution packaging, embedded code, dependencies, or public signing keys. The active target was corrected to SLES 12 SP3 after receiving its actual OS/binary/library identity on 2026-10-28. The same reviewed NRPE/user sources are rebuilt natively; their previous SLE-15 runtime observations do not prove SLE-12 compatibility. The port additionally builds the macros from pinned upstream sources and retains their BSD notice. Original SLE-12 dependency RPMs are verified but are not release assets. Historical releases are unchanged. Components in generated packages and sources Component Evidence inspected Findings and remaining work Debian nagios-nrpe Actual debian/copyright from the reconstructed custom sources for Debian 11 ( 4.0.3-1 ), 12 ( 4.1.0-1 ), and 13/14 ( 4.1.3-1 ); compared with the Debian 12 installed-package notice These four copyright files are identical. They declare GPL-2-or-later with an explicit OpenSSL linking exception for the main code; separate entries cover ACL code, snprintf , and Debian packaging. The full GPL text and upstream notice files are retained in the source archives. Recheck actual sources for every candidate; this is not a blanket approval of future source versions. This is evidence from the SLES source itself. The earlier search missed the word "exemption". Preserve the upstream notice and full GPL text ; see the source review . The short GPLv2 headings did not establish a GPLv2-only restriction. Retain Kaspersky Lab ZAO's 2011 copyright and the full per-file notices. Do not replace it with the project's MIT notice. Preserve the files and their notices in the source package. These exceptions are not evidence of an OpenSSL linking exception for NRPE. Nagios RPM macros 0.14 Immutable OBS revision a911087cc73b87e04465861110d43754 ; actual nagios-rpm-macros-COPYING and spec BSD-3-Clause, Lars Vogdt 2011. Retain the verbatim BSD notice , source RPM and complete original source set. The binary is a native build dependency, not a released runtime package. SUSE NRPE packaging Actual pinned nrpe.spec , including its SUSE LLC 2024 header Spec header retains contributed changes under the pristine package's license, subject to its stated fallback. Keep the original notice and modified spec in the source RPM; the project MIT license does not replace the spec's terms. system-user-nagios 1.0.0-0 Pinned manifest , revision b979817ae6424675519c86e80add617a ; actual original spec extracted from the source RPM and hash-verified Resolved: the source spec itself explicitly declares MIT and retains the SUSE LLC 2024 copyright/licensing header. The missing standalone full text is supplied as a downstream companion notice , not represented as an original upstream file or a new project license grant. Preserve the spec and README and include that notice in release assets. The SLES upstream archive is bound by SHA-256 7689aea570596573919371f7d6a1753eca90213368ede51f477e25782eb1ef9c . The manifests retain expected sizes and checksums for the original OBS input files; the exported source RPM contains the intentionally modified build spec. The earlier NRPE source RPM was unpacked and compared with the pinned manifest: 14 entries matched (including the intentionally modified spec), while the OBS history file nrpe.changes was absent. The companion source RPM matched its spec and README; system-user-nagios.changes was absent. Record these provenance differences explicitly. New SLES builds now export the complete original OBS input sets under obs-sources/ ; release preparation verifies every file against the pinned manifests and includes the history alongside the SRPMs. The original comparison alone is not evidence of a fresh build. The Debian 4.2.0-1 source review additionally covers the version now supplied by Debian 14. Its license grants and OpenSSL exception are unchanged; the Debian copyright edit removes obsolete FSF postal addresses. This does not approve later versions. Reviewed Debian upstream archive and license-file hashes are recorded in packaging/debian-license-review.json . Automatic publication fails for a new source version or changed evidence until it is reviewed; source discovery and local builds remain dynamic. This separates successful compilation from license review of previously unexamined source bytes. Host-only optional menu dependencies requirements-menu.txt pins prompt-toolkit==3.0.52 and wcwidth==0.2.13 . The renderer is installed separately, not vendored, bundled into NRPE packages or copied into the static site. Generated pages retain the licenses of their original documentation and notices. Bundling the renderer would require its actual license text and a separate dependency inventory. Website CSS, templates and browser JavaScript are independently authored project code; no external JavaScript framework, analytics SDK or font bundle is shipped. The build-only syntax highlighter is shiki@4.5.0 , pinned with integrity-checked transitive dependencies in website/package-lock.json . Installed shiki , @shikijs/core , @shikijs/langs , @shikijs/themes and @shikijs/engine-oniguruma LICENSE files were inspected and contain MIT terms; the installed @shikijs/vscode-textmate LICENSE.md also contains MIT terms. The original Shiki license is retained unchanged. Individual language/theme provenance is covered by the upstream grammar/theme notices . These dependencies, their grammars and WASM remain build-only, not vendored or included in NRPE packages or browser JavaScript. Generated code colors use the bundled GitHub Dark Default theme. The small NRPE syntax grammar and static HTML/CSS adapter are independently authored project code. The upstream NRPE sample configuration is referenced, not copied or relicensed as project code. Static diagrams use build-only mermaid@12.2.0 (MIT; the installed LICENSE was inspected and is retained unchanged ) and puppeteer@25.16.0 (Apache-2.0 in its package metadata), also locked with integrity hashes. The renderer uses the workstation's installed Chrome/Chromium and ships SVG output, not a browser binary, Mermaid runtime, fonts or Node dependencies. The previous Pygments renderer dependency has been removed. Docker images, OpenSSL, system libraries, Debian/SUSE repository packages, monitoring plugins, and SLES installation media retain their own licenses. The current release scope is the custom server packages, the SLES user package, their corresponding sources, and this project's build workflow. It does not include container images, dependency RPM/DEB bundles, or installation media. Any expansion requires an inventory of the additional shipped bytes. The bundled SUSE public key is trust material identified by the fingerprints and checksums in the SLES manifests. They are not independently authored project code; do not label them MIT merely because they are in this repository. Retain their issuer identity and provenance. Required release notices Each candidate must include this inventory, the project MIT license, and the actual notices from the source packages being distributed. Source archives must retain their full upstream and distribution license files. The generic GitHub repository source archive does not replace corresponding NRPE sources. For SLES, include the prepared notice directory as separate release assets alongside the unchanged binary and source RPMs. The review closes the previously recorded SLES OpenSSL, ACL-version and companion-MIT evidence gaps. It does not replace final candidate completeness and provenance checks. Keep the project's unofficial-build wording and NRPE's LEGAL trademark notice. title: Architecture and maintenance map
text: The host Python controller coordinates Docker Compose. Containers perform the actual package work; target packages are never installed on the development host. The optional terminal UI translates choices into the same CLI arguments used by automation. It does not bypass target locks or artifact validation. Run reports are local records, not cryptographically signed attestations. See the workflow reference for cleanup, stale locks, and report limitations. Shell is used for native package tools; Python is used for structured metadata and narrow source transformations. verify-sles-environment.sh checks the actual 12.3 identity and clean runtime base. The support-package build creates genuine macros/user RPMs; no dependency provides are faked. Terminal interaction lives in menu.py ; workflow execution remains in the controller. Server/companion checksums use one streaming helper in state.py , with the manifest read once per artifact inspection. Native SLES signature and identity verification lives in verify-sles-packages.sh ; the unused Python duplicate was removed. The legacy build.py remains a thin compatibility wrapper for existing callers, without its own workflow engine. Images and updates Builder images contain compilers and build requirements; runtime images contain only test/runtime prerequisites. A successful fresh-container install therefore cannot rely on a compiler or NRPE server preinstalled by the builder. Keeping two roles is intentional even when both derive from the same distribution base. Docker caches layers. --pull checks base images, while package-source updates are a different concern: Debian discovers sources through APT at build time; SLES uses explicitly reviewed pinned manifests. The controller does not yet compare a complete remote source/recipe identity to decide whether existing outputs need rebuilding. See repeatability .

title: NRPE configuration examples
text: These fragments illustrate a restricted deployment; they are not complete configuration files. Merge reviewed settings into /etc/nagios/nrpe.cfg on Debian or /etc/nrpe.cfg on SLES. Follow the official NRPE manuals for server/client setup, plugin installation and TLS provisioning. Never copy the project's test CA into production trust stores. NRPE file syntax and upstream defaults NRPE configuration uses flat key=value directives, full-line # comments, command[name]=... definitions and optional include / include_dir directives. It has no INI section headers. These examples use an NRPE-specific code grammar; general INI files use a separate grammar. The upstream sample nrpe.cfg.in is a build template , not the exact installed configuration for every package. Placeholders such as @pluginsdir@ , @sysconfdir@ and @nrpe_port@ are resolved when building/installing. Keep the configuration shipped with your distribution and NRPE version as the starting point. Do not copy upstream master wholesale onto an older daemon; supported directives and defaults can differ. The fragments below intentionally change selected settings for the described scenario. They are not a reproduction of upstream defaults, and do not replace the complete sample, included files or distribution-specific service setup. Hosts, TLS and fixed commands Example server settings, replacing the documentation IP and all certificate paths: allowed_hosts = 127.0.0.1,::1,192.0.2.10 dont_blame_nrpe = 0 allow_bash_command_substitution = 0 ssl_version = TLSv1.2+ ssl_use_adh = 0 ssl_client_certs = 2 ssl_cacert_file = /etc/nrpe-tls/monitoring-ca.pem ssl_cert_file = /etc/nrpe-tls/server.pem ssl_privatekey_file = /etc/nrpe-tls/server.key For this project's SLES 12 SP3 NRPE 4.1.1 build with RSA certificates, replace the ssl_version and ssl_use_adh settings above with all three lines: ssl_version = TLSv1.2 ssl_use_adh = 1 ssl_cipher_list = DHE-RSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384:!aNULL:!eNULL Keep the CA, server key/certificate and mandatory client-certificate settings. On this NRPE/OpenSSL combination, ssl_use_adh=0 also skips initialization of certificate-authenticated finite-field DH. The explicit cipher list permits only authenticated DHE-RSA with AES-256-GCM and excludes anonymous and null ciphers even though the initialization switch is enabled. This policy passed with 2048-bit DH and an OpenSSL 3.5.7 client using its default security level, server hostname/chain verification and a separate client certificate. Missing client certificates were rejected. Do not use ssl_use_adh=1 without the restrictive cipher list, and confirm that the actual monitoring client supports the chosen suite. These options do not apply to the old NRPE 2.15 daemon. The server certificate needs an appropriate identity and certificate chain. Give the NRPE service account the permissions necessary to read its key, without making that key readable by other users. Restrict incoming TCP 5666 to the actual monitoring hosts. Client-certificate verification and IP allowlisting have different roles; configure both. Do not reduce TLS settings to make an unconfigured client connect. Prefer fixed command definitions when caller-supplied arguments are unnecessary: command [ check_load_standard ] = /usr/lib/nagios/plugins/check_load -w 5,4,3 -c 10,8,6 command [ check_load_busy ] = /usr/lib/nagios/plugins/check_load -w 10,8,6 -c 20,16,12 These are illustrative thresholds, not capacity recommendations. Install your distribution's check_load plugin separately and locate its actual executable; SLES may use a different plugin directory. NRPE does not install every monitoring plugin. Keep command definitions and plugin/wrapper files owned by an administrator and unwritable by the NRPE account. From the monitoring host, a fixed check can be requested without -a : check_nrpe -H nrpe.example.internal -d 0 \ -A /etc/monitoring/tls/monitoring-ca.pem \ -C /etc/monitoring/tls/client.pem \ -K /etc/monitoring/tls/client.key \ -c check_load_standard Use your client's actual paths and the certificate-name verification options supported by its version. A successful encrypted connection alone does not establish that the intended peer identity is verified. Optional named argument profiles Enable this only for trusted authenticated monitoring clients when distinct fixed command names are unsuitable. NRPE substitutes $ARGn$ into a command before invoking its shell: a wrapper's argument validation happens after that substitution and is not, by itself, protection against shell injection. Preserve NRPE's default forbidden-metacharacter checks (including single quotes, backticks, backslashes, semicolons and newlines) and keep Bash substitution disabled. Do not loosen nasty_metachars , put untrusted text in command definitions, or expose this interface to arbitrary callers. The example wrapper accepts only standard or busy and maps them to fixed plugin options. Its first argument is an absolute plugin path fixed by the administrator in the server configuration; the caller does not select that path. It does not use eval , run a shell on received strings, or accept arbitrary plugin options. Install it after reviewing it: sudo install -d -o root -g root -m 0755 /usr/local/libexec/nrpe-custom sudo install -o root -g root -m 0755 examples/check-load-profile.sh \ /usr/local/libexec/nrpe-custom/check-load-profile Copy the reviewed example onto the destination first; that command assumes an examples/ directory in the current location. Test the locally installed wrapper as the service account with the actual plugin path before exposing it through NRPE. Example definition, using the Debian plugin path: dont_blame_nrpe = 1 allow_bash_command_substitution = 0 command [ check_load_profile ] = /usr/local/libexec/nrpe-custom/check-load-profile /usr/lib/nagios/plugins/check_load ' $ARG1$ ' Then request -c check_load_profile -a standard using the same client TLS options as above. Requesting unknown should return NRPE status UNKNOWN (3), without running the plugin. The wrapper preserves the plugin's OK/WARNING/CRITICAL exit status for accepted profiles. Additional wrapper arguments are rejected; do not add extra $ARGn$ placeholders to the definition. The unit tests exercise profile mapping, plugin exit status, and rejection of unknown/malformed arguments. They do not prove that a deployed NRPE configuration keeps its pre-shell protections intact. Test rejection of forbidden characters and unknown profiles in an isolated deployment before production use, and do not send destructive injection probes to production hosts. During introduction, both profiles, unknown-profile rejection and NRPE's pre-shell metacharacter rejection were also exercised over real TLS in a disposable Debian 12 container with the installed custom server. A fake load plugin recorded the exact options, so that check validates argument mapping and rejection, not the real plugin's load measurements or production capacity limits. Restart the relevant service after reviewing the configuration and verify checks from the real monitoring host. See installation , updates and rollback , and security .

title: Debian NRPE 4.2.0-1 source review
text: Reviewed on 2026-10-29 after Debian 14 source discovery selected 4.2.0-1 and publication correctly stopped at the unreviewed-source gate. Authoritative inputs The official Debian source pool supplies nagios-nrpe_4.2.0-1.dsc , its upstream archive and Debian packaging. Both archive sizes and SHA-256 digests were checked against the DSC: Input SHA-256 nagios-nrpe_4.2.0.orig.tar.gz f89455bdb5c4057d3bbebbde8a1d9f775d2598eb04d2d876eea9e718716e1a37 nagios-nrpe_4.2.0-1.debian.tar.xz 124df4d50457350c858f7f8e7951559ac8eff396db5d9beefc43e24a60a5e315 The comparison baseline was Debian's 4.1.3-1 source reconstructed with dpkg-source --extract ; its six recorded license-evidence hashes matched the existing review. These downloads used HTTPS. This comparison does not claim an independent verification of the uploader's DSC signature. Build-time APT archive authentication and source checksum checks remain required. License comparison LICENSE.md and LEGAL are byte-identical to the reviewed 4.1.3 source. debian/copyright only removes obsolete FSF postal-address paragraphs. The GPL-2-or-later grant, OpenSSL linking exception, ACL attribution, snprintf permission notice and Debian packaging license remain unchanged. Changed C/header files retain their existing copyright and license notices. In particular, src/acl.c and include/acl.h still explicitly grant GPLv2 or later. src/snprintf.c retains Patrick Powell's attribution requirement. src/utils.c:display_license() is byte-identical and explicitly permits compiling, linking and using OpenSSL. Changes elsewhere in that file do not change this grant. Upstream code, packaging and tests changed; this review records license evidence and does not substitute for build, installation or TLS testing. The exact upstream archive and six extracted evidence-file hashes are recorded in the publication allowlist . Publication still rejects unknown versions, changed upstream bytes or changed evidence. Full corresponding sources, GPL text and notices remain release assets. No source-version pin or bypass of the release gate was added.

title: Disposable VM deployment validation record
text: Template only: no VM scenario has been executed by filling in this document. Copy it for each target into an ignored local evidence directory, for example .nrpe/validation/debian12.md . Keep raw logs, certificates, keys, access details and configuration backups outside Git. Publish only reviewed, sanitized results. Follow the practical validation procedure , installation guide and rollback procedure . Do not use a production host. An actual VM snapshot and console/recovery access are prerequisites; a container is not a replacement for these tests. Identity and preparation Field Recorded value Tester / date / timezone Not recorded Target: debian11 / debian12 / debian13 / debian14 / sles12sp3 Not selected Disposable VM OS, release, architecture and image date Not recorded VM snapshot and tested console/recovery access Not prepared Workflow commit / published release tag Not selected Baseline binary package filename, exact installed version and SHA-256 Not recorded Candidate binary package filename, exact version and SHA-256 Not recorded Trusted checksum/signature verification Not performed Config/includes/permissions backup and original plugin paths Not prepared Separate monitoring client version and approved access rules Not prepared Test CA/server/client identities (no private material) Not prepared Pre-reboot / post-reboot boot IDs Not recorded Baseline and candidate must be two distinct real package versions. Verify and save the original binaries/checksums before starting; never rename an artifact to simulate an update. Read-only baseline inventory On the VM, record its actual identity and service definition. Use the correct branch below; these commands do not install packages or restart services: cat /etc/os-release uname -m cat /proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id getent passwd nagios Debian: dpkg-query -W -f= '${Package} ${Version} ${Architecture}\n' nagios-nrpe-server systemctl cat nagios-nrpe-server.service systemctl is-enabled nagios-nrpe-server.service systemctl is-active nagios-nrpe-server.service SLES 12 SP3: rpm -q --queryformat '%{NAME} %{VERSION}-%{RELEASE} %{ARCH}\n' nrpe systemctl cat nrpe.service systemctl is-enabled nrpe.service systemctl is-active nrpe.service On a fresh VM the package or service may not exist; record that outcome instead of treating missing baseline components as an installation pass. Save a baseline remote-check result with its exact command, TLS policy and exit status before any update. An already failing baseline TLS connection cannot prove successful remote-check recovery after rollback. Execute and record sequentially Use passed , failed , blocked or not run for each scenario. Fill in actual commands, exit codes, expected/observed results and reviewed evidence; do not prefill a success based on container CI. Order Scenario Status Expected / observed / evidence 1 Fresh install on a separate clean snapshot Not run Correct version, architecture, dependencies and real user; runtime arguments disabled 2 Service start and restart Not run Actual systemd unit active, expected listener, no configuration errors 3 Fixed real monitoring plugin Not run Runs as service user; local and remote output/exit status agree 4 Access, TLS and argument policy Not run Approved client works; invalid credentials/unapproved clients rejected; arguments rejected by default and accepted only after deliberate activation 5 Real VM reboot Not run Boot ID changes, service enabled/active, listener and authenticated remote check recover 6 Upgrade from verified baseline to distinct candidate Not run Expected package version; reviewed config prompts, includes/permissions retained; actual remote check passes 7 Package/configuration rollback Not run Original package and config restored; service and previously working baseline check recover; shared user package retained 8 Snapshot recovery, if necessary Not run Record separately; snapshot restoration does not prove package rollback Return to the required baseline snapshot between incompatible scenarios rather than carrying changes from the fresh-install test into an alleged baseline upgrade. A reboot or migration is performed by the operator only after reviewing the disposable VM identity, snapshot and recovery prerequisites. Completion and follow-up Overall result: not run . Failed/blocked scenarios and concrete reasons: not recorded. Restored final state and temporary network/certificate cleanup: not recorded. Reviewer and sanitized evidence references: not recorded. Update the release plan only with actual results for the exact tested OS and artifacts. Leave other targets open. Windows Docker Desktop validation uses its own procedure and is not established by completing this VM worksheet.

title: Frequently asked questions
text: Find answers about services, TLS and supported builds. Start with the running service before changing packages; for log analysis, see troubleshooting . Search the FAQ Clear search Installation & services Does a separate NRPE agent also need Nagios Core locally? TLS & certificates NRPE checks on SLES: services first, then SSL/TLS Versions & builds Which SLES version does this project target? What happened to SLES 15 SP3 and SP4? When do I actually need a custom build? No answers match your search. Try a shorter term, such as “TLS”, or clear the search to browse all questions. Installation & services Does a separate NRPE agent also need Nagios Core locally? # No. Nagios Core schedules checks on the monitoring server. Its check_nrpe client contacts the NRPE daemon on the monitored host, which executes the configured local plugins. A host used only as an NRPE agent needs its NRPE daemon and required plugins, but does not need a local Nagios scheduler. Starting Nagios alone does not start a separately packaged NRPE daemon. The two-service command applies to the combined server, not every NRPE agent. See the connection map for the separate roles. TLS & certificates NRPE checks on SLES: services first, then SSL/TLS # Check the managed NRPE service first. On a combined Nagios/NRPE server, both services must run. If the connection still fails, compare the client and daemon versions and their TLS configuration before considering a custom build. These questions belong to the same troubleshooting sequence. The operator later clarified that starting the missing nrpe.service resolved the checks in their combined Nagios/NRPE setup. A custom package was not needed for that service availability problem. Start with the intended service and listening process, then investigate TLS only if the connection still fails. A stopped daemon cannot itself negotiate TLS; an SSL-handshake message from an NRPE process shows that a process was running at that time. Historical logs, a manually started daemon and the current systemd state can describe different moments or different listeners. Which services must run on a combined Nagios and NRPE server? When Nagios Core and the NRPE daemon are installed on the same SLES server, and the installed units are named nagios.service and nrpe.service , enable and start each service: sudo systemctl enable --now nagios.service sudo systemctl enable --now nrpe.service systemctl is-active nagios.service nrpe.service enable --now configures startup at boot and starts the service immediately. Both should report active for this combined setup. Nagios schedules checks; NRPE independently listens for and executes remote plugin requests. If a unit is missing or fails, inspect the installed unit names and logs before replacing packages: systemctl list-unit-files nagios.service nrpe.service sudo systemctl status nagios.service nrpe.service --no-pager sudo journalctl -u nagios.service -u nrpe.service -n 100 --no-pager Package-provided service names vary. For the custom Debian server package in this project, the NRPE unit is nagios-nrpe-server.service : sudo systemctl enable --now nagios-nrpe-server.service Follow the official Nagios Core documentation and NRPE documentation for complete installation and deployment configuration. Enabling a service does not install missing plugins, provision TLS credentials or configure monitoring checks. Before interpreting an SSL error, also confirm which process owns port 5666: sudo ss -ltnp 'sport = :5666' If a manual test daemon still owns the port, an enabled systemd unit alone does not prove it is serving requests. Restore the intended managed instance before retrying the same check from the monitoring server. For a persistent failure, continue with the version/TLS checks below. Why does the old SLES 12 NRPE daemon fail its SSL handshake? If the managed daemon is active and requests still fail, compare versions and TLS policy. The original reported server ran NRPE 2.15-4.24 , linked to OpenSSL's 1.0 ABI. That old NRPE advertises anonymous DH, not modern certificate authentication. A newer NRPE/client built for SLES 12 can use certificate-authenticated TLS 1.2 with the original OpenSSL 1.0.2 library. TLS 1.3 requires a newer TLS library and is not provided by this build. disable_syslog=0 is unknown to the old daemon; commenting it out removes the warning but does not fix TLS compatibility. The message Could not complete SSL handshake. 1 alone does not identify a specific cipher, certificate or trust failure. Compare the actual server/client versions, command, TLS settings and simultaneous logs. Do not disable encryption or certificate verification to hide the error. Build-time --ca-cert affects source downloads, not the deployed NRPE certificate configuration. To isolate this on SLES 12 SP3 before upgrading, the temporary plaintext diagnostic documents the user's successful NRPE 2.15 / check_nrpe 4.1.0 test on a separate port. It includes anonymized examples, the encountered errors and cleanup; it does not recommend disabling TLS in production. For NRPE 4.1.1 on SLES 12, also review the authenticated DHE-RSA example . With this old OpenSSL integration, ssl_use_adh=0 skips DH initialization and can produce no shared cipher with modern clients. Use the complete documented policy, which explicitly excludes anonymous ciphers, rather than enabling ADH alone. It was tested against OpenSSL 3.5.7 with certificate verification intact. Versions & builds Which SLES version does this project target? # SLES 12 SP3 , confirmed by /etc/os-release . The active target is sles12sp3 ; see the native build guide . What happened to SLES 15 SP3 and SP4? # Those targets came from an incorrect assumption about the affected server's OS. It was subsequently identified as SLES 12 SP3 with NRPE 2.15 and OpenSSL 1.0.2. The active SLES-15 Dockerfiles, manifests, media setup and target guides have been removed. There is no supported SLES-15 build target in the current workflow. The remaining explanation is consolidated here. Historical release results and dated license/maintenance observations retain their original platform labels in the release history and linked reviews. They do not prove SLES 12 compatibility, and old SLE-15 RPMs must not be installed on SLES 12. The cleanup command still recognizes old local output names solely to remove them explicitly; CLI tests reject those names as build targets. These references do not restore SLES-15 support. When do I actually need a custom build? # Use the distribution package when it already provides the required feature. A custom build makes sense when a required compiled feature is missing. Before rebuilding, distinguish service/configuration problems from missing features: Check that the intended NRPE service is running and inspect its logs. Confirm the monitoring server can reach NRPE with the intended allowed hosts, firewall rules and TLS configuration. Confirm that the configured plugin exists and runs as the NRPE service user. If arguments are required, check both the package's compiled support and the runtime policy. dont_blame_nrpe=0 intentionally rejects arguments even when support was compiled in. Enable arguments only after reviewing the command definitions and validating permitted inputs. A stopped service or an argument-disabled runtime setting alone is not a reason to compile another binary. This project's Debian build is for deployments that deliberately need compiled command-argument support; it preserves disabled runtime arguments by default and disabled Bash command substitution. After changing configuration, restart the applicable NRPE service and repeat the actual remote check. enable --now does not restart an already active service to reload modified configuration. See installation and deployment security for this project's custom package scope.

title: Branches, commits and integration
text: master is the default and release branch. develop is the integration branch. Never delete either branch. New work starts from current develop on one of feat/... , fix/... , refactor/... , or remove/... . git fetch origin git switch develop git pull --ff-only origin develop git switch -c feat/example # Make and test the change, then stage explicit paths and commit. git push -u origin feat/example gh pr create --base develop Use a PR/MR into develop . Promote the tested integration branch using a PR from develop into master ; never route a topic directly into master . Prefer a normal merge for develop-to-master promotion so ancestry remains clear. Keep working on topic branches, not directly on either long-lived branch. Integration ends at develop by default. Create or merge a develop-to-master promotion PR only when the maintainer explicitly requests promotion to master. A request to implement a change or integrate it into develop does not authorize a master PR or release. Once an explicitly requested promotion reaches master, the automatic release workflow runs as configured. By default, work remains on a local topic branch. Pushing, opening a PR or merging into develop requires an explicit maintainer request. Master promotion requires its own explicit request. Complete the current change and checks before starting the next integration. Attribution Commits carry the existing human author identity. Do not add co-author trailers, AI attribution, or generated-with/by lines. Never rewrite old history to change attribution. The policy check rejects invalid routes, recognizable bot identities, missing author identities and attribution trailers. Git metadata alone cannot prove that an author is human; maintainers must review it. Dependabot PRs are proposals targeting develop , not exceptions to this policy. Review their changes and bring approved updates onto a correctly named topic branch with the human author's commit before integration. Do not merge bot-authored commits or automatically merge update PRs. Topic branch cleanup gh-pages is the website deployment branch, not a topic branch. Website sources follow the normal topic-to-develop review flow; an explicitly requested publication appends a human-authored generated-site commit to gh-pages. It does not promote develop to master. See website publication . Leave GitHub's unrestricted Automatically delete head branches setting off. It cannot express the required distinction between topic branches and the long-lived develop head of a promotion PR. The cleanup workflow handles successful merges into develop only. It requires an eligible topic prefix, the same repository, no other open PR needing the head, and an unchanged head SHA. Deletion uses a Git lease so a concurrent push is not deleted accidentally. Unmerged/closed PRs, forks, changed heads and unknown branch prefixes are retained. master and develop are always excluded. After a successful merge, update local develop , inspect local changes and PR state, and remove the corresponding local topic only when its work is integrated. Never use gh pr merge --delete-branch for a develop-to-master promotion. Legacy branches outside the named prefixes are not automatically removed. Server-side protection: one-time administrator action The ruleset template protects both long-lived branches against deletion and force-pushes, requires PRs and resolved review threads, and requires the branch/author policy and all fast CI checks. It does not impose an extra reviewer count on a single-maintainer repository. Protection was applied by the repository owner and verified on 2026-10-27: active ruleset 25987752 targets refs/heads/master and refs/heads/develop , with no bypass actors. Both branches have deletion/force-push protection, PR and resolved-thread requirements, and all six fast status checks from the template. The default branch remains master ; unrestricted automatic head-branch deletion is off. Inspect effective rules when checking or changing repository settings: gh api repos/NoJokeFNA/nrpe-custom/rules/branches/master gh api repos/NoJokeFNA/nrpe-custom/rules/branches/develop For a new repository, an administrator can apply the template through GitHub's Rules/Rulesets settings or API, subject to plan and permissions. The connected integration returned HTTP 403 for administrative writes; owner configuration was required. Inspect existing rules before applying a template to avoid duplicates. Keep both target branches selected, the ruleset active, default branch master and global head-branch deletion disabled. Repository settings are separate from workflow guards; verify both rather than assuming that a committed template establishes protection. See release automation for what a master push does.

title: Installing a custom NRPE package
text: Run these commands on the destination Linux server. Python, Docker, and this checkout are needed on the build workstation, not on the destination server. Use a package built for the destination's distribution release and architecture. The current SLES target is SLES 12 SP3 x86_64 , not every SLES 15 service pack. For the complete NRPE server/client and Nagios setup, use the official NRPE documentation and Nagios Core documentation . This guide covers deployment of the custom packages and essential configuration checks; it does not replace those manuals or distribution-specific plugin and TLS instructions. Prepare the files Build and test the selected target on the workstation with, for example, python3 nrpe.py verify debian12 or python3 nrpe.py verify sles12sp3 . Copy the following files into a dedicated directory on the destination server: Destination Build output directory Files to copy Debian 11 output/debian11/ nagios-nrpe-server_*_amd64.deb , SHA256SUMS Debian 12 output/debian12/ nagios-nrpe-server_*_amd64.deb , SHA256SUMS Debian 13 output/debian13/ nagios-nrpe-server_*_amd64.deb , SHA256SUMS Debian 14 output/debian14/ nagios-nrpe-server_*_amd64.deb , SHA256SUMS SLES 12 SP3 output/sles12sp3/ nrpe-*.x86_64.rpm , system-user-nagios-*.noarch.rpm , monitoring-plugins-nrpe-*.x86_64.rpm , SHA256SUMS Keep exactly one server package version in that directory so the wildcards below select the intended package. Source RPMs, manifests, and Debian build information are useful provenance but are not installed on the destination. Change into the directory containing the copied files and verify them: sha256sum --check SHA256SUMS Continue only if every entry reports OK . Copy the checksum file through a trusted channel alongside the packages; checksums detect changes but do not authenticate the publisher by themselves. Keep all three SLES binary RPMs available for this check even if the destination already has the user package installed. For releases that include SHA256SUMS.sig , first perform the release authentication check using an independently trusted maintainer key before extracting/installing packages. Unsigned releases are identified in the release history . If NRPE is already installed, back up its configuration before updating. Review package-manager prompts about configuration files and dependencies. Preserve the site's command definitions, allowed monitoring hosts, and TLS configuration. Package installation may start or restart a service. For an existing deployment, follow updates and rollback before replacing packages. The configuration examples and maintenance policy describe optional checks and verification boundaries. Debian 11, 12, 13, or 14 Check the destination release and architecture: cat /etc/os-release dpkg --print-architecture The architecture must be amd64 . Use the package from the matching Debian output directory; a Debian 12 package is not a package for every Debian release. From the directory with the verified .deb file: sudo apt update sudo apt install ./nagios-nrpe-server_ * _amd64.deb dpkg-query -W -f= '${Package} ${Version} ${Architecture}\n' nagios-nrpe-server APT resolves runtime dependencies through the destination's configured Debian repositories. The explicit ./ selects the local custom package. Confirm that the installed version contains +withargs1 (or the custom revision of the build you selected); the upstream version itself is discovered at build time. Edit /etc/nagios/nrpe.cfg using your preferred editor. Review the configuration steps below before restarting. sudo systemctl enable nagios-nrpe-server sudo systemctl restart nagios-nrpe-server sudo systemctl status nagios-nrpe-server --no-pager If startup fails, inspect the service log: sudo journalctl -u nagios-nrpe-server -n 100 --no-pager SLES 12 SP3 Check the destination release and architecture: cat /etc/os-release uname -m Expect SLES 12.3 and x86_64 . The current pinned build produces: nrpe-4.1.1-0.withargs1.x86_64.rpm system-user-nagios-1.0.0-0.noarch.rpm The destination must actually be SLES 12.3 x86_64. Do not install a SLE-15 package or replace the system OpenSSL. Retain the old NRPE 2.15 package and back up the main configuration, includes, plugins and TLS files before upgrading. The newer package retains /etc/nrpe.cfg as a configuration file; review package prompts and any .rpmnew / .rpmsave files rather than assuming that defaults replace an existing deployment's policy. Use your authorized matching SLES-12 repositories for missing runtime dependencies. Review the package requirements and user package first: rpm -qp --requires ./nrpe-4.1.1-0.withargs1.x86_64.rpm rpm -q system-user-nagios The minimal test image additionally needs original libwrap0 and util-linux-systemd ; a full server may already provide them. Resolve missing prerequisites using the destination's matching repositories, for example: sudo zypper refresh sudo zypper install libwrap0 util-linux-systemd shadow netcfg grep sed coreutils Then install the verified local artifacts with normal RPM dependency and payload checks. If no suitable user package exists, install the companion and server in one transaction: sudo rpm --upgrade --verbose --hash \ ./system-user-nagios-1.0.0-0.noarch.rpm \ ./nrpe-4.1.1-0.withargs1.x86_64.rpm If a suitable user package is already installed, keep it and install the server: sudo rpm --upgrade --verbose --hash ./nrpe-4.1.1-0.withargs1.x86_64.rpm These are locally built unsigned RPMs. Verify their hashes through a trusted channel (or the optional release signature when enabled) before installation. Never use --nodeps , --nosignature or global repository signature bypasses. This project's test does not bypass missing dependencies. SLES 12's zypper does not provide the newer --allow-unsigned-rpm option used in some SLE-15 examples. The matching client RPM is available for a SLES 12 SP3 monitoring host : sudo rpm --upgrade --verbose --hash ./monitoring-plugins-nrpe-4.1.1-0.withargs1.x86_64.rpm It needs the same real Nagios user and matching runtime libraries. Do not install that client RPM on another distribution; use its native client package instead. All three binary files are needed to check the unchanged SHA256SUMS , even when only the server/user package will be installed on the monitored host. Confirm the installed server and user: rpm -q nrpe getent passwd nagios Expect nrpe-4.1.1-0.withargs1.x86_64 for the current build. zypper install nrpe without the local filename can select the repository package instead of this custom build. Edit /etc/nrpe.cfg using your preferred editor. Review the configuration below before restarting: sudo systemctl enable nrpe sudo systemctl restart nrpe sudo systemctl status nrpe --no-pager If startup fails: sudo journalctl -u nrpe -n 100 --no-pager Configure and start NRPE Distribution Configuration Service Debian /etc/nagios/nrpe.cfg nagios-nrpe-server SLES 12 SP3 / OBS recipe /etc/nrpe.cfg nrpe Argument support is compiled in, but dont_blame_nrpe=0 remains the packaged default. Keep it at 0 if the monitoring server should not supply arguments. To deliberately enable them, edit the existing settings in the appropriate configuration file, for example: allowed_hosts = 127.0.0.1,::1,192.0.2.10 dont_blame_nrpe = 1 Replace 192.0.2.10 with the actual monitoring server address. Define permitted commands and validate any $ARG1$ , $ARG2$ , etc. they accept. Configure production TLS authentication and allow incoming TCP 5666 (or your chosen server_port ) only from the intended monitoring servers. Keep Bash command substitution disabled. See deployment security and network requirements . Restart the distribution's service after changing its configuration, using the commands above. A successful service start does not prove argument handling or remote connectivity; exercise the configured check from the real monitoring server with the intended TLS settings and arguments. The project's container tests do not validate the destination's systemd, firewall, or production TLS. The build-time --ca-cert option configures repository HTTPS trust inside build and test containers. Its CA is not embedded in the exported package and does not provision the destination's NRPE certificates, keys, or operating-system trust. Review future package-manager upgrades: a repository package can supersede a local custom version. After upgrades, confirm the installed custom revision again and rebuild from reviewed sources when security updates are needed.

title: Cleaning local workflow data
text: clean previews eligible data by default. It does not install packages, change the target server, remove current packages or contact Docker unless an image is explicitly selected. The terminal menu exposes the same options under Local cleanup . It shows the read-only preview before a separate deletion confirmation, defaults to cancellation and rejects a changed candidate list until it is previewed again. python3 nrpe.py clean python3 nrpe.py clean --older-than 60 --keep-runs 10 The defaults are 30 days and at least five retained runs. Only completed, recognized run directories containing report.json and optionally run.log are candidates. Both completion time and file modification times must be old enough. Running, malformed and unrecognized evidence is left for inspection. The newest report for each current target and the newest test report matching its current package bytes are retained even with --keep-runs 0 . The newest complete successful verify report matching those bytes is also retained, even if a newer runtime-only test exists. Current target output directories, release candidates, downloaded releases, locks, certificates and arbitrary working directories are never cleanup candidates. Back up evidence you need beyond that retention policy before deleting it. Apply an inspected selection python3 nrpe.py clean --older-than 60 --keep-runs 10 --apply --apply is explicit deletion consent, including in non-interactive use. The tool recalculates the plan under a maintenance guard; changed candidates abort the operation. Active or unresolved target locks block deletion. New controller workflows cannot acquire target locks during cleanup. Symlinks, Windows reparse points and special files in traversed cleanup paths are rejected. Mounted candidate directories and nested mount points are rejected too. Cleanup is sequential, not a filesystem transaction: an I/O or Docker error can leave a partially completed cleanup. Already removed paths are reported. Inspect the error and preview again; do not assume everything was deleted. Direct Compose commands do not take controller locks. Do not run them against the same workspace while applying cleanup. After a crash, a retained .nrpe/locks/maintenance directory must be inspected along with processes and containers before manually removing that marker. Never remove a live lock. Retired SLES output Include expired output for the explicitly retired sles15sp3 and sles15sp4 targets only when requested: python3 nrpe.py clean --retired-outputs python3 nrpe.py clean --retired-outputs --apply The same age threshold applies. A retired directory with an unknown top-level file is retained for manual review. The active sles12sp3 and Debian outputs remain protected. This does not remove published SLE-15 releases or their historical verification evidence from GitHub or Git. Individually selected Docker images python3 nrpe.py clean --image nrpe-custom-builder:sles15sp3 python3 nrpe.py clean --image nrpe-custom-builder:sles15sp3 --apply Repeat --image to select more than one explicit nrpe-custom builder/test image tag. Docker is required for the preview too. Base images, bare IDs and wildcards are rejected. Images used by running or stopped containers are refused; identity and usage are checked again before applying. Removal uses docker image rm without force. A concurrent Docker change can still cause Docker to refuse deletion; the tool does not override that protection. This command does not prune Docker globally or remove containers, networks, volumes or BuildKit caches. Removing an image tag may reclaim little space when layers are shared. Manage Docker Desktop/Engine storage separately if necessary.
