title: Support and maintenance policy
text: This independent open-source workflow has best-effort maintenance, without an SLA, guaranteed response times, enterprise support rights, or an extension of a distribution's lifecycle. See the warranty notice . Scope and verification Area Project scope and verification Debian 11–14, amd64 Matching build/runtime containers, source export, package validation and TLS tests; a successful run verifies its exact package bytes SLES 12 SP3, x86_64 Genuine SP3 basis, pinned OBS sources, server/client, real user RPM and build-macros source; other SLES service packs are not covered Linux host CLI Standard-library CLI and optional menu; hosted unit-test CI Windows host CLI Hosted Python unit tests; Docker Desktop Linux-container operation and actual console behavior need separate practical verification macOS / ARM hosts Linux/amd64 emulation may work; outside the hosted host matrix and not verified by Linux/Windows results Production deployment Installation guidance and examples; operators configure plugins, monitoring, systemd, access, TLS and recovery Python 3.9 remains the application minimum. CI exercises that minimum and Python 3.14 on Linux/Windows, not every intermediate interpreter or terminal. The optional audit tool has its own Python 3.10+ minimum and is not an application dependency. Use an upstream-maintained interpreter for production; compatibility testing does not provide security maintenance for an interpreter. Consult the Python version lifecycle . Fast CI runs units, shell syntax and Compose checks. The separate release workflow runs the full package/install/protocol matrix on master pushes and release-relevant PRs. Workflow configuration is not proof of a pass: inspect the actual run for the commit being evaluated. The practical validation procedure tracks the separate Windows Docker Desktop and Debian/SLES VM checks for console, company CA paths, systemd, reboot, plugins and update/rollback behavior. Historical archives/repositories may become unavailable. Consult Debian release information and SUSE lifecycle information for current upstream maintenance status. An archived target that still builds does not necessarily receive dependency security fixes. Never silently substitute another suite, SLES service pack, or Leap packages to preserve a passing result. Automated dependency monitoring Dependabot checks Python requirements, locked website npm dependencies and GitHub Actions version tags weekly and proposes update PRs into develop , without automatic merging. Bot proposals need human-reviewed/authored integration under the Git policy . Actions use official major-version tags such as actions/setup-python@v6 , as selected by the maintainer. Dependabot proposes major-version changes through PRs; compatible updates within the selected upstream major tag are picked up directly. The repository owner may need to enable Actions/Dependabot in GitHub settings; checkout configuration does not override those settings. The dependency audit runs weekly, on relevant requirement changes, and manually. Pinned pip-audit checks menu requirements and resolved dependencies against published advisories. Findings and collection failures fail the job. It does not scan NRPE C code, DEB/RPM contents, system libraries, container images or SLES repositories. A clean result is not a security certification. The separate website check audits requirements-website.txt and validates generated documentation and publication guards. The renderer is isolated from the NRPE CLI/menu environment. To reproduce the audit using Python 3.10+ in an isolated development environment: python3 -m venv .venv-audit .venv-audit/bin/python3 -m pip install -r requirements-audit.txt .venv-audit/bin/python3 -m pip_audit --strict -r requirements-menu.txt On Windows use .venv-audit\Scripts\python.exe for the environment-local commands. Keep the audit tool separate from the optional menu environment. Human review cadence At least monthly during active maintenance, and before a release: Review relevant upstream NRPE announcements, fixes and advisories, Debian package changes, and SUSE security information for the deployed versions. Review update PRs and audit findings. Assess affected deployments promptly rather than waiting for routine review; record mitigations and review dates. Reassess target lifecycle/repository availability. Explicitly deprecate a target when continued validation is no longer feasible. Rebuild affected targets and run fresh install/TLS tests after source, dependency or recipe changes. Unit/Compose checks alone are insufficient. This is a maintainer procedure, not an installed reminder or a claim of continuous security-feed monitoring on behalf of users. The 2026-10-27 review records actual upstream, advisory, dependency and lifecycle findings, with outstanding actions and the next review date. Record later reviews separately rather than overwriting that evidence. Reviewing source and recipe updates Debian discovers its suite's official source version at build time. --pull refreshes base images, not an existing exported package's source identity. Preserve previous outputs, then explicitly rebuild and verify updates. Do not automatically replace SLES revisions/hashes. Review authoritative source and packaging changes, signatures and license terms, then update the manifests and checksums together. Retain pure SP3 dependencies, runtime-disabled arguments and disabled Bash substitution. Change the custom revision when modifying the recipe for the same upstream version. Revisit license evidence when source versions or grants change. For both formats, retain source/binary version identity, export corresponding sources, and validate every affected target. Never rename a binary to manufacture a version. Follow the release plan before publication. Deprecation and reporting Before removing a target, document the reason, last actually verified versions and run date, planned removal boundary, and any separately verified replacement. An untested suite/service pack is not a drop-in replacement. For non-sensitive bugs, provide host OS/architecture, Python, Docker Engine, Compose and Buildx versions, target, command/flags, expected behavior and a redacted log excerpt. Include artifact/run identity where relevant. Do not attach keys, company certificates, credentials, full environments or configuration backups. Follow security reporting guidance for vulnerabilities. Use updates and rollback for deployments. Recovery on a real server is distinct from rebuilding a package in a container.

title: Interactive terminal menu
text: The menu is an optional frontend to the same controller used by direct commands. It does not implement separate build, locking, or cleanup behavior. The workspace overview shows package presence, the latest recorded outcome and Docker readiness from the last explicit check. It never checks Docker merely by opening the menu, or treats package presence as a successful verification. The screenshot is an actual prompt_toolkit render of an empty temporary workspace, not evidence of a package build. Use direct commands for automation; see the CLI help capture for the command list. Install and start From the repository root, install the pinned host-only dependencies: python3 -m pip install -r requirements-menu.txt python3 nrpe.py If your Python installation is managed by the operating system, use a virtual environment instead of overriding its package protections: python3 -m venv .venv Activate with . .venv/bin/activate on Linux/macOS, or .venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1 in PowerShell. Then run the installation command above. The active interpreter must be available as python3 . If a Windows virtual environment does not provide that alias, use its explicit interpreter .venv\Scripts\python.exe for both pip and nrpe.py , or configure a local python3 alias for it. No particular editor is required. The menu uses prompt_toolkit for terminal input and rendering. This dependency is not installed in build containers. Direct commands such as python3 nrpe.py verify debian12 continue to use only the Python standard library. Controls Key Action Up / Down Move selection; long lists scroll Home / End Jump to the first / last item Enter Select an action or accept selected targets Space Toggle a target in the multi-selection screen A Select all currently visible targets, keeping previous selections / Start filtering labels and descriptions; type letters, including Q Backspace Edit the filter Tab Keep the filter and return to selection shortcuts ? Toggle contextual keyboard help Escape / Q Go back; Esc first closes help or clears an active filter; Q is literal text while filtering Ctrl+C Exit the menu; during a workflow, interrupt its command and clean up its container Ctrl+D End the menu at a selection prompt Selections and filtering are retained when returning to a directory or the workspace. Long lists scroll to the highlighted entry; labels stay on one row so a long path cannot consume the file list. Details provide contextual help. Complete paths are available in a separate scrollable view. During a workflow, the live panel shows the current controller phase, phase/run elapsed time, per-target states and a bounded tail of recent output. No percentage is guessed. Full Docker output is still written to the run log. Dispatch and cancellation stay on the main thread; only rendering runs in a background thread. The result screen offers target details, full logs and diagnosis of that run. Inspection commands and full logs remain in terminal scrollback until Enter or Esc returns to the menu. Logs are also available with logs --run <id> . Workflow Choose build and test, build only, or test existing packages. Select one or more named distributions with Space, then Enter. The first workflow has no selection; later workflows retain the session selection. Choose whether to refresh base images for a build. Existing-package tests omit that build option. Optionally browse for a public PEM/DER company CA certificate, or enter/paste its path directly. Esc returns to targets. Review the action, targets, base-image refresh, certificate path and output replacement. Cancel is selected by default; Back to options preserves all choices. SLE-15 media selection was retired. Select Run. Existing outputs are rebuilt only after this explicit confirmation. Read the recorded per-target result, inspect full logs or explain a failure, then return to the workspace. The certificate default follows NRPE_CA_CERT , if configured. The options show whether the choice came from the environment, was selected manually, or was explicitly disabled. Invalid environment defaults are validated before review. "Do not use a company CA" overrides the environment for this session, without changing it; direct commands can use --no-ca-cert . The CLI rejects combining that option with --ca-cert . Choices are kept only in memory until the menu exits. This CA trusts build downloads. It does not configure NRPE server/client certificates or Docker Engine/registry trust. See company CA trust for scope and image-cache details. Diagnostics and cleanup Diagnostics checks Docker explicitly or explains a recorded/local log. For a local file, choose build/download or NRPE context and state whether a build CA was supplied. Diagnosis reads text; it never runs log content or changes TLS. Runs are filterable by date/ID, target, action and outcome. Local cleanup exposes retention age, number of runs to keep, retired outputs and optional explicit project image tags. It uses the same planner and guards as the cleanup CLI . Preview is read-only and remains visible before a separate confirmation, with cancellation selected by default. Changed candidates require another preview. There is no Docker-wide prune or forced removal; current packages and retained evidence remain protected. Diagnostics, status, and logs are available from the workspace. A failed command returns to the menu after its result is acknowledged. Closing the menu does not turn a failed workflow into a passed run: inspect its exit message, report, or status. For automation, use direct commands and their exit codes rather than the menu session's exit code. Enter or paste a path The certificate browser includes Enter or paste a path... . A file selects that certificate; a directory opens that location. A direct certificate-path option is also available from the source menu. Paste paths as plain text, for example C:\Certificates\Company Root.cer , or with matching quotes as copied by Explorer's Copy as path . Backslashes and spaces are preserved; paths are never evaluated as shell commands. ~ and native environment-variable syntax are expanded (for example %USERPROFILE% on Windows). Relative paths entered in a browser are relative to its current directory; direct source-menu entry is relative to the process working directory. Tab offers path completion. Enter accepts; Escape or an empty value cancels. Cancelling returns to the existing browser location. Missing paths and incorrect file/directory types show an error with options to retry or cancel. Certificate contents still undergo regular validation. Many drives and long paths Windows drive letters appear only in Switch drive... , not in every directory. For twelve attached drives, the file list still contains just the current folder, its navigation actions and eligible files. The separate drive selector is scrollable and filterable with / ; enumeration uses the OS drive mask without probing every drive for labels, capacity or connectivity. Only the selected root is opened. Unavailable roots show an error and retain the previous directory. Cancelling drive selection retains the browser's folder, selection and scroll position. Returning to a parent directory restores its highlighted entry. Use Show complete current path for long paths or Enter or paste a path... for direct drive/UNC access. Linux keeps ordinary directory/mount navigation. Terminal behavior Use an interactive terminal on Windows, Linux, or macOS. NO_COLOR requests monochrome rendering; selection remains visible through an arrow and reverse video, rather than color alone. TERM=dumb also disables color, but a terminal with cursor-control support is still needed for the menu. Use direct commands for restricted terminals, screen-reader workflows where full-screen interfaces are unsuitable, redirected output, and CI. With no terminal attached, launching without arguments prints CLI help without importing the optional dependencies or prompting. If a terminal is attached but the dependencies are missing, the CLI prints the installation command. Validation limits for this revision Keyboard/filtering/session-state tests, simulated 0/1/12-drive and unavailable-root tests, and an actual Linux PTY cancellation exercise passed locally. The PTY exercise used simulated build output to check main-thread interruption, retained logs and lock release; it was not a real package build. Real Windows Terminal, mapped/network drive and Docker Desktop scenarios remain not run here; use the practical validation checklist .

title: Network and firewall requirements
text: Separate build-time downloads from production NRPE traffic. Builds require outbound access, not an inbound NRPE port on the workstation. The default integration test keeps both client and server inside one container over loopback. Connection map Connection map · Open full size View diagram source flowchart LR H[Workstation / Docker daemon] -->|HTTPS 443| REG[Image registries, authentication, and blob storage] C[Build and test containers] -->|HTTP 80 or HTTPS 443| PKG[Distribution package repositories] C -->|HTTPS 443| OBS[OBS source and RPM API] TC[Test client inside container] -->|TLS TCP 5666 over loopback| TS[Test NRPE inside same container] N[Production Nagios server] -->|TLS TCP 5666 by default| P[Production NRPE target] Outbound destination inventory Prefer hostname-aware rules or an approved proxy/mirror. The following is a starting inventory derived from the recipes, not an exhaustive static allowlist. Registry/repository responses may redirect to other download hosts; resolve those through your approved network policy. Do not disable TLS or signature checks to work around a firewall rejection. Hosts Ports Used by Purpose github.com TCP 443 Git client Clone/update this repository; GitHub releases if used later registry-1.docker.io , auth.docker.io TCP 443 Docker/BuildKit Official Debian/Python input-stage images and Dockerfile frontend image/authentication production.cloudflare.docker.com , production.cloudfront.docker.com TCP 443 Docker/BuildKit Possible Docker Hub blob/CDN destinations; actual endpoints may differ registry.suse.com TCP 443 Docker/BuildKit Genuine SLES 12 SP3 image; follow authorized registry authentication/blob endpoints deb.debian.org , security.debian.org TCP 80 and/or 443, matching image APT sources Debian containers Package indexes, NRPE source, build and runtime dependencies archive.debian.org TCP 80 in the current Bullseye security rewrite Debian 11 containers Archived security packages; APT authenticity checks remain enabled api.opensuse.org TCP 443 SLES input-download stage Pinned OBS sources, pinned original SLE-12 Server/SDK RPMs; authoritative signing keys during reviewed updates pypi.org , files.pythonhosted.org TCP 443 Host pip, only when installing the optional menu prompt_toolkit and wcwidth The default SLES-12 native build and runtime steps install local pinned inputs; they need no repository registration or network access after input preparation. Custom registries or APT mirrors change the workstation's outbound destinations. The controller does not supply subscription credentials or accept terms. Configured DNS resolution is also required. Use your network's DNS resolver and policy (commonly UDP/TCP 53); no particular public DNS service is required. TLS environments may additionally require access to certificate-validation services specified by their certificates and local policy. Why there is no fixed public IP list These domains use CDNs, geographic mirrors, authentication services, and changing A/AAAA records. An IP returned today can become incorrect or belong to a shared service. GitHub's published IP ranges do not cover all registries and package mirrors. A one-time DNS lookup is therefore not a durable or least-privilege rule. If the firewall accepts only destination IPs, use an approved internal HTTP(S) proxy or registry/package mirror with managed addresses. Allow clients to reach that internal service, and maintain its external destinations centrally. Internal IP addresses and credentials belong in site configuration, not this repository. Integration tests The client connects to 127.0.0.1:5666 inside the test container using TLS. No Compose service publishes this port to the Docker host. No incoming TCP 5666 rule is needed on the build workstation. The temporary configuration permits only loopback. It does not alter production allowed_hosts , certificates, or firewall rules. Test image creation and package installation still need the outbound package access described above, unless an approved cache/mirror supplies it. Production NRPE Source Destination Rule Explicit Nagios/poller IPs NRPE target server Allow TCP 5666 inbound on the target, or your configured server_port NRPE target Established monitoring connection Permit return traffic through the stateful firewall Allow only the actual monitoring servers, including their effective source address after NAT where applicable. Use those addresses in NRPE's allowed_hosts and configure TLS authentication. NRPE does not normally initiate a new connection back to Nagios. Additional connections required by individual check plugins are deployment-specific and outside the protocol's port requirement. The target server may separately need outbound package-repository access during installation and updates. See deployment security . Proxies and diagnosis Docker image pulls, BuildKit downloads, host pip, and programs inside running containers are separate clients. Configuring a host proxy alone does not prove that every layer can reach its dependencies. Use supported Docker daemon/Desktop proxy configuration and Docker client proxy/build configuration as appropriate. For TLS inspection, install your organization's trusted CA in each affected client/base image; preserve certificate verification. python3 nrpe.py doctor checks local Docker readiness and Compose configuration. It does not probe every remote repository. Inspect the failing phase's log with python3 nrpe.py logs --last and your proxy/firewall logs to identify an actual blocked hostname or redirect. Do not share unredacted authenticated URLs, repository credentials, or complete proxy configuration files. When a Docker command fails and its output contains a recognized TLS/certificate error, the CLI prints a troubleshooting hint and saves it in the run log. For certificate verification errors it indicates whether a company CA was supplied, and points to --ca-cert or the menu's certificate selection when none was given. A hint identifies a possible cause; it does not prove a company CA is missing. Image pulls and Dockerfile frontend downloads require Docker/BuildKit trust configuration separately. Successful commands and unrelated failures do not produce a TLS hint; the original output and exit code are preserved. Optional company CA certificate If your organization inspects HTTPS traffic, the containers must trust the organization's issuing CA. For errors such as Curl error 60 / self signed certificate in certificate chain , select the public root or intermediate CA provided by your administrator: python3 nrpe.py verify sles12sp3 -- ca - cert "C:\Certificates\Company-Root.cer" python3 nrpe.py test debian12 -- ca - cert "C:\Certificates\Company-Root.cer" The option is supported by build , test , verify , and build.py , for every target. The menu includes a certificate file browser under Workflow options. Alternatively set NRPE_CA_CERT to the local file path; the explicit --ca-cert option takes precedence. With neither configured, no extra CA is added. Use --no-ca-cert to explicitly omit the company CA even when NRPE_CA_CERT is set; it cannot be combined with --ca-cert . The menu offers the same session-only override without changing the process environment. Supply one public X.509 certificate , in PEM or DER format. .cer , .crt , and .pem filenames are supported; the contents determine the format. Bundles and private keys are rejected. This is a CA for repository HTTPS, not a production NRPE client certificate or key. Keep your file outside the checkout, or under the ignored local-certificates/ directory. Do not commit company trust material. The controller validates and normalizes the certificate in memory and passes its PEM contents through the child process environment as a BuildKit secret. No temporary certificate file or Windows TEMP path enters the Compose-to-Bake handoff. The internal NRPE_CA_PEM variable is set only for the Docker child process, using the validated certificate (or an empty value without a CA). The normalized SHA-256 is passed separately to invalidate the image cache when the certificate changes and is recorded in report.json ; its contents are not logged. Debian builder and test images install the selected certificate in their system trust stores before contacting repositories. SLES-12 input downloads add it only to their in-memory Python TLS context; the native stages are offline. Debian's minimal-image bootstrap preserves existing roots until the regular CA package regenerates the full trust database. TLS, APT/zypper signatures, and source checksums stay enabled. For Debian, the installed CA and generated trust database remain in local image layers, including Docker caches. Do not publish company-specific builder/test images without your organization's approval. The CA is not embedded into the exported NRPE package. Run subsequent commands without the option/environment variable to build images using only their default trust; existing cached images are not modified in place. The option configures container trust. It cannot fix registry pulls that fail before the Dockerfile runs , because Docker Desktop/Engine and BuildKit use separate trust stores. Configure those through your organization's Docker instructions if required. Host pip/Git trust is also separate. Use nrpe.py to prepare the secret and its cache identity; direct Compose commands do not normalize DER input or calculate that identity for you.

title: Practical validation beyond container CI
text: These checks cover host and service behavior that the automated package/TLS matrix does not exercise. Use disposable hosts and test certificates. Follow the installation guide , upstream NRPE documentation and update/rollback procedure for deployment details. Current evidence and result recording The published SLES 12 SP3 release passed all five container build/install/TLS and source/archive gates plus Linux/Windows Python unit tests. Exact release and commit evidence, including the earlier SLE-15 scope, is retained in the release history . Windows Docker Desktop and real VM scenarios below remain not run . On 2026-10-28 the current cloud environment had no /dev/kvm , QEMU/libvirt or supplied test-VM access. The maintainer confirmed that no test VMs are available. These scenarios are prepared for later execution, not replaced by container or hosted Windows unit tests. Do not run package migration/reboot tests on a production server to fill this gap. For each scenario record passed, failed, blocked or not run, with: Date, tester, exact Git commit/release tag, package version and SHA-256. Host OS/release/architecture, Python, Docker Engine, Compose and Buildx versions where applicable; VM image/release and service unit for deployment tests. Scenario, command, expected/actual outcome, exit status and run ID. A redacted failure excerpt and follow-up issue when a check fails. Keep full run reports, private paths, configuration backups, company certificates and keys outside Git. Share only reviewed, sanitized evidence. A pass applies to the tested host/artifacts, not automatically to every supported platform. Windows Docker Desktop Use an actual Windows host with Docker Desktop's Linux engine. Record the shell and terminal; include Compose 5.6.1 and Buildx 0.38.1 when reproducing the original report, then test current supported versions separately. Use a clean checkout in a path containing spaces and non-ASCII characters, for example C:\NRPE validation\Project Ω\nrpe-custom . Put a public test CA certificate in a different such directory; never pass a private key to --ca-cert . These are illustrative test paths, not required installation locations. The Ω deliberately exercises Unicode handling; use real folders and certificate paths on your test host. From that checkout in PowerShell: python3 -- version docker version docker compose version docker buildx version python3 nrpe.py doctor python3 nrpe.py verify debian12 -- ca - cert "C:\NRPE validation\Company CA Ω\company-ca.pem" -- pull $LASTEXITCODE python3 nrpe.py status python3 nrpe.py logs -- last Use your actual certificate path. The expected result is a complete successful build/install/TLS run, with no temporary-path failure at "load local bake definitions". For intentional repeat builds of existing output, add --rebuild . title: Release signature setup and verification
text: SSH Ed25519 signatures authenticate the release's SHA256SUMS manifest using an independently trusted maintainer key. That manifest covers all five target archives, workflow sources, notices, metadata and notes. This signs the release bundle; it does not add DEB/RPM package signatures or certify software safety. Rollout status Signing support is included in the published SLES 12 SP3 release. No production signing key is enrolled in packaging/release-allowed-signers . Signing remains off until the maintainer completes enrollment, configures the secret/variable and explicitly requests promotion to master. The releases recorded in the release history are unsigned; enrollment does not retroactively authenticate them or replace their files. GitHub's artifact attestation requirements require Enterprise Cloud for private repositories. This repository is private; the connected integration's attestation API read returned HTTP 403, so account entitlement/access is not established. The SSH approach needs neither that service nor disclosure to a public transparency log. Repository visibility stays unchanged. No signing key or secret is generated or configured by this change. Enroll a maintainer-controlled key Use OpenSSH 8.2+ with ssh-keygen -Y signature support. On a trusted workstation, outside the checkout, create a dedicated key if none exists: ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -N '' -C nrpe-custom-release -f ./nrpe-release-signing ssh-keygen -lf ./nrpe-release-signing.pub The CI key must be unencrypted for noninteractive use. Protect its private file and backup; do not reuse an administrator/login key or commit the private key. Only the .pub file and its SHA-256 fingerprint are public enrollment material. On an allowed topic branch, add the actual public key to packaging/release-allowed-signers using this format: text nrpe-custom-release namespaces="nrpe-custom-release" ssh-ed25519 BASE64_PUBLIC_KEY Review the key and fingerprint independently and integrate through a PR into develop. Consumers need that trusted public key independently of release files. With owner-authorized GitHub credentials, configure the repository secret and variable from the trusted workstation, using the actual private-key path: sh gh secret set NRPE_RELEASE_SIGNING_KEY --repo NoJokeFNA/nrpe-custom < ./nrpe-release-signing gh variable set NRPE_RELEASE_SIGNING --repo NoJokeFNA/nrpe-custom --body ssh-ed25519 Run the local signing/verification check below with a candidate directory. Promote develop to master only on the maintainer's explicit request. Verify that the resulting release contains SHA256SUMS.sig and passes consumer verification before marking enrollment complete in the release plan. The publishing job writes the secret to a temporary mode-0600 key file, signs, verifies against the reviewed signer list, then removes the temporary key. The local CLI restricts the temporary directory to the current Windows SID before writing a key on Windows; POSIX uses a mode-0700 directory. The key is unavailable to PR/build/test jobs. A missing/mismatched key, empty trusted signer list or unsupported signing mode stops publication when signing is enabled; there is no fallback to an unsigned release. An unset variable or explicit off retains checksum-only publication and logs that signing is off. Changing this setting is an administrative decision, not an automatic recovery step after a signing failure. For key rotation, enroll and independently communicate the new public key before switching the CI secret. Preserve independently trusted old public keys for historical releases. If a key is compromised, revoke consumer trust and assess affected releases; simply changing the workflow key does not revoke old trust. Consumer verification Obtain the signer file from a trusted checkout or independent maintainer channel and confirm its fingerprint independently. A public key shipped alongside an untrusted download does not authenticate that download. Download all release assets into one otherwise empty directory, including SHA256SUMS.sig . From a trusted checkout containing the verification helper: python3 scripts/release_signature.py verify --directory /path/to/downloaded-release \ --allowed-signers /path/to/trusted-release-allowed-signers The helper first authenticates the checksum manifest, then requires the exact asset set and verifies every payload hash. It rejects missing signatures, unknown signers, extra/missing files, links, invalid checksum paths and changes. It does not extract or install packages. Treat any nonzero exit as failure; unsigned historical releases cannot pass this authentication check. The equivalent signature-only OpenSSH command on a POSIX host is: ssh-keygen -Y verify -f /path/to/trusted-release-allowed-signers \ -I nrpe-custom-release -n nrpe-custom-release \ -s /path/to/downloaded-release/SHA256SUMS.sig \ < /path/to/downloaded-release/SHA256SUMS That command authenticates the manifest only. The Python helper additionally checks completeness and hashes. On Windows, use a recent OpenSSH installation and the Python helper; PowerShell redirection is not a substitute for the POSIX stdin example above. Local signing check For a complete candidate produced by release preparation , the signing CLI accepts the name of an environment variable containing the private key. It never accepts the key itself as a command-line argument: NRPE_LOCAL_SIGNING_KEY = "$( cat /secure/path/nrpe-release-signing)" \ python3 scripts/release_signature.py sign --directory .nrpe/release \ --allowed-signers packaging/release-allowed-signers --key-env NRPE_LOCAL_SIGNING_KEY Use a shell with tracing disabled. Test using disposable keys for development; never upload private keys or logs containing them. Signing refuses an existing signature rather than replacing it. Signing and verification commands do not upload or publish anything.

title: Per-push package releases
text: Each push to master runs the release workflow . The repository's visibility is unchanged. Topic/develop pushes do not publish releases. Release-relevant PRs run the build and archive checks without publishing; manual workflow dispatch is also validation-only. Build and publication gate Run the Linux/Windows unit matrix, shell/Compose checks and dependency audit. Build all five targets on separate fresh Ubuntu runners: Debian 11, 12, 13, 14 and SLES 12 SP3. Apply this project's packaging changes through the normal builders. Install each package in its matching disposable runtime container and test disabled/enabled arguments over TLS. All targets are attempted even if one fails; no release is published unless every target succeeds. Record the clean workflow commit before and after verification, plus hashes of binaries and exported source assets. A runtime-only test, dirty checkout, stale report, changed artifact or missing source/notice fails preparation. Validate Debian DSC references, source/binary versions, reconstructed rules and license files. Validate all three SLES source RPMs against binary identities and pinned original inputs. Export all original OBS files, including .changes history, alongside the modified source RPMs. Package each target, then require exactly the five expected target archives. Verify their entries, target/commit identities, notices and checksums; reject traversal, links, duplicates, missing/extra files and oversized archives. Add the exact Git workflow source archive, license inventory, release manifest, notes and checksums. Verify uploaded-asset checksums again in the publishing job. Upload to a draft first and publish only after all uploads succeed. Only the master push publishing job receives write permission. No bot commits are created: a release tag points to the already-reviewed workflow commit. Optional SSH release signing authenticates the checksum manifest before publication when explicitly configured. Enrollment and actual signed-release validation are separate from implementing the helper; see its rollout status. Creating or merging a master promotion requires an explicit maintainer request; routine integration stops at develop. Assets and naming The release tag is build-<workflow-run-number>-<commit-prefix> . This identifies every successful master push without inventing a semantic version policy or renaming distribution packages. Package versions remain the versions recorded by Debian changelog/SLES spec, including the project's custom revision. Release assets are: nrpe-custom-debian11.tar.gz through nrpe-custom-debian14.tar.gz . nrpe-custom-sles12sp3.tar.gz . workflow-source.tar.gz , LICENSE , THIRD_PARTY.md , release.json , RELEASE_NOTES.md , and SHA256SUMS . SHA256SUMS.sig when SSH signing is enabled. This detached signature is not part of its own signed checksum manifest. Target archives contain the original package filenames, installation checksum manifest, corresponding sources, component license notices and a sanitized verification manifest. SLES includes matching server/client RPMs, the real user package, the build-only macros source RPM and all three original OBS input sets. Debian includes its custom DSC and referenced original and packaging archives. The workflow source includes the required build scripts, recipes, manifests and original per-file notices. Raw logs, environment values, CA/media paths and .buildinfo files are excluded from published verification data. Company trust material, private keys, container images, dependencies and SLES media are not release assets. Actions retains the prepared archives for 14 days; published GitHub release assets are separate. An older concurrent build cannot replace a newer commit's latest release. Published assets are immutable in this workflow: rerunning an already published run fails rather than clobbering its tag or files. An interrupted upload can leave a draft; inspect and remove that incomplete draft/tag deliberately before rerunning. No partial target subset is presented as a complete release. Local candidate preparation Use a clean committed checkout. Install ordinary inspection tools ( dpkg-dev , rpm , rpm2cpio , cpio ) on the inspection runner, not custom output packages on the workstation. After a fresh python3 nrpe.py verify <target> run: python3 scripts/prepare_release.py target --target debian12 \ --commit "$( git rev-parse HEAD)" --destination .nrpe/target-bundles Repeat for all five targets, then: python3 scripts/prepare_release.py assemble --commit "$( git rev-parse HEAD)" \ --incoming .nrpe/target-bundles --destination .nrpe/release Use new/empty staging directories; existing archives are not silently replaced. Old reports without source/workflow identity cannot be used for releases. The stage/verify commands do not publish anything. Use the Git workflow to review and integrate changes before promoting develop to master . Builds still depend on reachable distribution/OBS repositories and registry availability. A failed download, signature, TLS or protocol check stops publication; it does not trigger an insecure fallback. Successful container tests do not prove production systemd, TLS, firewall or monitoring configuration is correct. Follow installation , rollback and the support policy on real systems.

text: Reviewed on 2026-10-27. The same exact upstream and companion source inputs are reused for the SLES 12 SP3 migration on 2026-10-28. Their short "License: GPLv2" headings do not replace those full grants. The notices retain Kaspersky Lab ZAO's 2011 copyright and are consistent with Debian's GPL-2+ entry. Checked file hashes: File in the pinned archive SHA-256 include/acl.h 323ca78733e229c77ec4e8a37fdc837b47558af11776660753b98023e83e138a src/acl.c 73f223aeec851559738d06aa2a4e26319c33300d53082d67f0d8a1fc3ae5ef00 Preserve these original headers in the source RPM; no relicensing or replacement copyright notice is necessary.
